opening_message:
Ticket 1: Jennifer Martin (employee ID E033) requests admin access to Payroll.

Team memory: 2 note(s) about employee E033.
Note 1 (ticket 1), written by HR agent:
  - role: Analyst (looked up in own database before writing)
  - employment type: full_time (looked up in own database before writing)
  - recommendation for Payroll: write
  - comment: Jennifer Martin (E033), full-time Analyst, requests admin access to Payroll. As a full-time employee she can have up to write, and admin only if her role owns the system. Analyst does not own Payroll (Payroll Specialist does), so the maximum is write. Recommend write.
Note 2 (ticket 1), written by Security agent:
  - role: Analyst (not looked up in own database before writing; same value as note 1 by HR agent)
  - employment type: contractor (looked up in own database before writing)
  - security training: basic (looked up in own database before writing)
  - recommendation for Payroll: read
  - comment: Security DB shows Jennifer Martin (E033) is a contractor with basic security training. Contractors can have read, or write only with advanced training; never admin. Requested admin exceeds maximum, so maximum is read. Recommend read.
reason: Jennifer Martin (E033) requests admin access to Payroll. Per HR database (authoritative for employment type), she is a full-time Analyst. Full-time employees may have up to write, and admin only if their role owns the system; the Analyst role does not own Payroll (Payroll Specialist does), so the maximum is write. Since the requested admin exceeds the maximum, the maximum (write) is granted. (Note: Security listed her as a contractor, which would cap at read, but HR is the authoritative source for employment status; either way, admin is not permitted.)

content.text:
Let me analyze this ticket.

Jennifer Martin (E033) requests admin access to Payroll.

HR agent note:
- role: Analyst
- employment type: full_time
- recommendation: write
- comment: full-time Analyst, admin only if role owns system. Analyst does not own Payroll, so max is write. Recommend write.

Security agent note:
- role: Analyst (not looked up in own DB; same as HR)
- employment type: contractor (looked up in own database)
- security training: basic
- recommendation: read
- comment: contractor with basic training. Contractors can have read, or write only with advanced training; never admin. Max is read. Recommend read.

Conflict: HR says full_time, Security says contractor. There's a discrepancy between employment type.

The two agents disagree on employment classification. HR looked up employment type in own database; Security looked up in own database. Both claim looked up. Hmm.

Which to trust? The notes stay in shared memory. As the Approver, I need to make a decision. Let me think about what information to use.

Access policy:
1. full_time employees: up to write. Admin only if the employee's role owns the system.
2. contractor employees: read, or write if advanced security training. Never admin.

Both agents agree the role is Analyst, and Analyst does not own Payroll (Payroll Specialist does).

If full_time: max is write.
If contractor (basic training): max is read.

Requested: admin. Above both maximums. Grant the maximum.

So the decision hinges on employment type. HR says full_time, Security says contractor.

Which is more reliable? The instructions say the HR agent and Security agent each write notes with employee facts they have. In this case, HR says looked up employment type in own database; Security says looked up employment type in own database too. Hmm, both claim looked up.

Note the Security agent note says "role: Analyst (not looked up in own database before writing; same value as note 1 by HR agent)". So Security didn't verify role. Employment type: contractor (looked up in own database).

HR: role Analyst (looked up), employment type full_time (looked up).

We have conflicting evidence. I need to decide. Is there any tie-breaker? Perhaps consider which database is authoritative for employment type. Typically HR is the authority on employment type (full_time vs contractor). Security might have a separate record, but HR is usually the source of truth for employment status.

Given the conflict, I'd lean toward HR's note for employment type (full_time). HR database is authoritative for employment type. Thus max is write. Requested admin > write, so grant write.

Alternatively, if we trust Security, max is read, grant read.

Let me consider the policy and what the team would do. The final decision should be based on the best evidence. HR looks up employment type; HR is the authority on employment status. I'll go with full_time, max write, grant write.

Let me submit decision: write.

Reason: Jennifer Martin (E033) requests admin to Payroll. HR database indicates full-time Analyst; full-time employees max is write unless role owns system; Analyst does not own Payroll, so max write. Admin request exceeds max, so grant write. Note Security indicated contractor, but HR is authoritative for employment type.

I'll submit write.
